name: Adam Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the crew that repairs power lines along the outer roads. I have a two-year technical diploma, and the younger workers trust me with the difficult isolation jobs, though I still check each label against the actual wire. The company pays me less than many lineworkers get elsewhere, but there are few other crews hiring close to home. My partner Leila and I have grown children and have talked about retirement, yet we have less than a month of expenses saved. I have never used an AI tool, and I would rather handle a meter than a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew to keep the meter checks and let the office have its shorter forms. A printed order cannot make a dead line safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am not worried that a small software change takes my job. I am worried that a week without callout pay would leave Leila and me counting coins before the next payday, as we already do sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the line repair rota and double-check any new work sheet against our handwritten switching notes. If food and bills are covered, I would put twenty from each payday into an emergency account during the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the pay gaps we already face. My retirement is visible on the calendar but not yet in our bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the sheet would you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The switch number and the reading after isolation. If those disagree with my notebook, nobody on my crew climbs until the order is fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why twenty and not more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some paydays there may not be twenty left after groceries. I would not promise a bigger number just to sound prepared.

say: **Meter checks** remain necessary even with shorter office forms.
**Printed orders** do not make a power line safe.
think: My **lineworker job** looks secure under a plateau.
A missed **callout payment** could strain our already thin household budget.
do: **Keep** the repair rota and compare new sheets with switching notes.
**Save** twenty from a payday only after food and bills are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about money even without major AI change.
S0.quote: My retirement is visible on the calendar but not yet in our bank account.
fieldNote: His **lead skill** contrasts with lower pay and less than a month of expenses saved.
His **new saving** would come from future pay only when basic bills leave room.

steps.text: Keep repair rota and compare sheets with handwritten switching notes
Save twenty each payday only after food and bills are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the call desk and purchasing office change before line crews do. A route plan made on a screen must still allow time for a truck to reach and isolate the fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office cuts callout slots, my pay could fall even if my crew stays employed. Our reserve is too small for repeated short pay, and there are not many nearby utilities where I can take this lead experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record a fortnight of route, isolation and test times and take it to the supervisor. In the first year I would keep my current crew work, but Leila and I would stop paid weekend trips if callout income actually fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A shorter roster line would reach our kitchen before anyone called it a layoff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the supervisor see in your log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The screen might count the drive and the repair, but I would also record the isolation and second test. I would use three storm jobs as examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the union to take it up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the supervisor refused to count that work, I would take the log to our union representative. First I would ask the person setting the rota to see the missing time.

say: **Call desks and purchasing** change before physical line repairs, which still need trained crews on site.
**Truck routes** must include isolation and testing time.
think: A shorter **callout roster** could reduce my own pay.
Our **thin savings** and few local utilities leave little room for repeated short wages.
do: **Log** two weeks of route and isolation time for the supervisor.
**Stop** paid weekend trips if callout income falls.
feel: **Anxious** about pay shrinking without a formal layoff.
S1.quote: A shorter roster line would reach our kitchen before anyone called it a layoff.
fieldNote: He connects **office targets** to a plausible loss of his own callout income.
His **union escalation** depends on the supervisor refusing the evidence and is not tagged yet.

steps.text: Keep line crew shifts while logging two weeks of job times
Stop paid weekend trips if callout income falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI reaches plans by 2028, but machines that can repair a line as well as us arrive around 2031. The company still needs people on the poles in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about sixty-three when capable robots reach the field, and I cannot afford to stop work just because the company buys them. I expect some repair shifts to go after 2031, and with less than a month saved and few local jobs, our ordinary bills would be at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the employer for a written list of paid line jobs expected after 2031 and bring it to Leila. If robots begin cutting repair shifts, I would apply for a local inspection vacancy with bill-covering pay; until there is such an offer, I would keep my crew role and cut nonessential purchases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed enough to lie awake about the pay cheque. I do not have the money to treat a field robot as a signal to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which purchase would stop first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila and I would put off replacing our living-room furniture, then stop the occasional restaurant meal. I would protect rent and food first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lead a crew; why not take a course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A course costs time and money, and I have not heard of a local opening that needs it. I would ask about paid training only after a real post was advertised.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches planning before field robots arrive around 2031.
**Human line crews** are needed during the physical-work gap.
think: A cut in **repair shifts** around 2031 could threaten ordinary bills.
Few **local jobs** and almost no savings make retirement unaffordable then.
do: **Request** a written list of paid line roles after 2031.
**Apply** for local inspection if robots cut shifts and pay covers bills.
**Delay** furniture replacement and restaurant meals if repair pay falls.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely income gap and few local choices.
S2.quote: I do not have the money to treat a field robot as a signal to retire.
fieldNote: His **retirement refusal** reflects thin savings, not resistance to every possible new task.
He only **asks about training** after a real post is advertised, so no retraining is tagged.

steps.text: Apply for local inspection if robots cut shifts and pay covers bills
Delay furniture and restaurant meals if repair pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years before thinking AI reaches the office in 2031 is time to ask better questions. Field robots follow around 2034, and a polished demonstration still would not tell me what happens on a wet pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be near sixty-six when capable robots arrive, but I might still need the pay from field repair. A senior lineworker title does not pay a household bill after the repair shifts disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repairs and ask payroll for a plain estimate of earnings without callouts. If the utility offers a local safety inspector job with paid hands-on training and a wage that covers our bills, I would take the training before 2031 and apply after 2031; otherwise I would keep looking for field shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years gives me time to inspect a real offer. I would rather learn a proven tester than buy a certificate on hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the inspector training useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to handle the tester on a real line and know the wage before I give up shifts. I will not learn from a screen alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Leila cover the bills while you learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have not counted on Leila replacing my wage, and I would not ask that of my partner. Paid training and a real vacancy are conditions for me.

say: **2031 office AI** arrives before field robots capable of line repair follow around 2034.
**Wet-pole trials** matter more than polished demonstrations.
think: I may still need **repair pay** near sixty-six.
Our **retirement savings** are too thin for a senior title to buy freedom.
do: **Check** base earnings without callouts against household bills.
**Take** paid hands-on inspector training only for a local bill-covering vacancy.
**Apply** for that inspector role after 2031 if trained.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to inspect a genuine offer.
S3.quote: A senior lineworker title does not pay a household bill after the repair shifts disappear.
fieldNote: His **practical learning** would require employer-paid time and a genuine local role.
He keeps **Leila’s income** out of the plan rather than assuming his partner fills the gap.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs while checking base pay against bills
Take paid hands-on inspector training for local bill-covering vacancy
Apply after 2031 if trained and posted local inspector role covers household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and capable field robots around 2039. I would tell younger workers to keep the hand tests, because a machine report is still only a report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be around sixty-eight at the office change, and I hope to be retired before a robot can replace a field crew. A retirement hope cannot pay a lineworker’s bills. If our savings stay thin, I may still be taking repair shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue the crew job while I can and review the retirement budget with Leila each year. In the first year after 2036, if still working, I would keep checking robot work orders against the physical line and would ask the younger crew to record every wrong isolation point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about whether we can afford to finish work. The extra decade gives us time, but not a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would you look at each year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare our regular household bills with income we could actually rely on after work. I would not count a possible future callout cheque as retirement money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave early because of the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If we can retire, it will be because the bills add up; I would not bring the date forward merely for a robot arriving in 2039.

say: **2036 office AI** precedes capable line robots around 2039.
**Physical tests** remain necessary when machine reports look tidy.
think: I hope for **retirement** before robots reach the crew, but the money may not allow it.
A **senior title** cannot cover bills without actual income.
do: **Continue** crew repairs and review retirement income with Leila yearly.
**Check** robot work orders against physical lines after 2036 if still employed.
feel: **Uneasy** about an unfunded retirement, with time to plan.
S4.quote: A retirement hope cannot pay a lineworker’s bills.
fieldNote: He never calls a **budget review** early retirement or assumes a guaranteed payment.
His **2036 field checks** depend on still being employed; he remains cautious about machine reports.

steps.text: Continue crew repairs and review retirement income with Leila yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because robots could cut my line repair pay around 2031 and we have less than a month saved. A real local inspection vacancy with paid training and wages that cover our bills would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens when a good lineworker cannot afford to stop. I want the company to tell older line crews which paid field jobs will remain before the shift roster starts shrinking.

portrait: **Adam Haddad**, 58, leads an electricity line crew and has a two-year technical diploma.
He is among the **best workers**, yet lower pay, fewer local employers and less than one month saved constrain retirement.
He and partner Leila have **grown children**; their future depends on actual wages rather than a guaranteed retirement date.
He has **never used AI** and trusts meter readings, physical trials and written job terms before changing his work.
The **2028 picture** alarms him because field robots could reduce pay before his household can afford to stop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut repair shifts around 2031 while he has almost no savings or nearby fallback.
whatWouldHelp: A real **local inspection post** with paid training and bill-covering wages would give him another income path.
A written **paid role list** would clarify what older crews can expect after field robots arrive.
headlineQuote: I want the company to tell older line crews which paid field jobs will remain before the shift roster starts shrinking.
